name: Color corrector (peach/orange)

lead: A peach or orange color corrector is a pigmented cosmetic layered under concealer or foundation to cancel blue-purple shadows under the eyes. The brighter, more even under-eye is visible straight away.

It works on color theory: a warm tone opposite blue-purple on the color wheel neutralizes the dark area so it sits closer to the surrounding skin. Wikipedia describes related approaches such as yellow undertones for dark circles and green for redness. Periorbital hyperpigmentation itself is described as an inherited melanin trait.

paras: People dab a small amount onto the darkest part of the under-eye, blend it lightly, then apply concealer or foundation over it. Deeper skin tones tend to use deeper orange shades, lighter tones peach. It lasts for the day and comes off with makeup removal.

The effect is temporary and sits on the skin surface; it does not change the cause of dark circles. No safety data specific to peach correctors were found. As with any cosmetic near the eyes, irritation or allergy to an ingredient is possible.

web.title: Kosas Revealer Color Corrector review - Today.com

angle.text: Users layer a peach or orange corrector under concealer to cancel blue-purple under-eye darkness, and the brighter look is visible right away. It is a cosmetic technique that lasts for the day.

lead: A peach or orange color corrector is a pigmented cosmetic applied under concealer or foundation to cancel out blue-purple or brownish discoloration, most often the darkness beneath the eyes. Users apply it so that tired-looking, shadowed under-eyes read closer to the surrounding skin tone, which gives a brighter, more rested face within minutes.

The approach rests on color theory: orange sits opposite blue on the color wheel, so a warm layer neutralises a cool dark tone before a skin-colored concealer goes on top. Makeup brands describe peach shades for lighter and medium skin and orange or orange-peach shades for deeper skin.[1] Wikipedia describes the related practice of using yellow undertones for dark circles, green or blue to counter redness and purple to brighten sallow skin, and does not mention peach or orange by name.[2]

Under-eye darkness has several causes. Periorbital hyperpigmentation is described as a hereditary trait involving extra melanin in the skin around the eyes, most common between ages 16 and 25.[3] Correctors act on how the area looks rather than on its cause, and they wear off when removed. No published studies of peach or orange correctors were found.
infobox: Peach, orange; related yellow, green, purple correctors [2]
Concealer or foundation applied over it [1]

paras: Color correctors are sold as creams, sticks and liquids in shades such as peach, orange, pink, yellow and green, each aimed at a particular tone.[1] Concealers more broadly come in liquid, stick, cream, pencil and cream-to-powder forms and are often used with foundation.[2]

Peach and orange correctors extend the layered approach to deeper under-eye discoloration. In a Today.com product review, the brand Kosas is described as offering pink, peach and orange correctors for blue-purple and green under-eye discoloration, with a peach for light-medium to medium-deep skin and an orange-peach for medium-deep to deep skin.[1]

For under-eye concealing, Wikipedia says people typically choose a shade one or two levels lighter than their skin, often with yellow undertones, and set it with powder to reduce creasing.[2] The Today.com reviewer describes placing small amounts of corrector at the inner, middle and outer under-eye, blending, and layering concealer on top rather than mixing the two; she says earlier correctors she tried were too pigmented or hard to blend and left her looking pink or peach.[1]
Brand and reviewer accounts are the main source on technique; no clinical guidance on peach correctors was found.
Correctors are surface makeup. No safety data specific to peach or orange correctors were found, and as with any cosmetic the reaction depends on the product and the skin.
Max Factor introduced Erace in 1954, described as the first commercially available concealer.[2]
